short_statement: For FCFS multiserver jobs, saturated-system throughput gives an exact finite-state criterion with Poisson arrivals and phase-type durations. Seek compact or polynomial-complexity criteria and broader input models.
full_statement: Consider a system with $N$ identical servers and $K$ job classes. Class $k$ jobs arrive according to a renewal or Poisson process of rate $\lambda_k$, require $b_k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ servers simultaneously, and have service-time distribution $S_k$. Jobs wait in a single first-come-first-served queue. When the job at the head of the line requires at most the currently idle servers, it starts service and occupies $b_k$ servers for its service time; otherwise it blocks later jobs even if those later jobs would fit. Let $X(t)$ describe the ordered waiting line, jobs in service, and residual service/interarrival information needed to make the process Markov. For independent Poisson class streams, let $\lambda=\sum_k\lambda_k$ and sample each new job's class with probability $p_k=\lambda_k/\lambda$. With phase-type durations, an exact criterion already exists: $\lambda<\lambda^*(p)$, where $\lambda^*(p)$ is stationary completion throughput of the saturated FCFS system, which replaces each departure immediately and keeps $N$ jobs present. Its finite CTMC can be solved by balance equations. The remaining computational target is a compact closed form or a characterization polynomial in the primitive class/server description, not merely finite-state enumerability. General renewal streams or non-phase-type service require separate assumptions and cannot automatically be replaced by i.i.d. Poisson job marks.
known_results: Wang, Xie, and Harchol-Balter emphasize that even the exact stability region is very hard, and they derive sufficient conditions for zero queueing in large-system scaling regimes. Grosof, Harchol-Balter, and Scheller-Wolf give a closed-form stability region for the two-class FCFS multiserver-job system with distinct server requirements and exponential service distributions. Grosof, Hong, Harchol-Balter, and Scheller-Wolf (Performance Evaluation 162, 2023, article 102378), Sections 2.2 and 3, describe the saturation-rule criterion for Poisson arrivals with i.i.d. joint server-need/phase-type-duration marks. Appendix C computes the threshold from finite balance equations. Theorem 4.2 further gives mean response time to additive $O(1)$ as arrival rate approaches that threshold. Thus exact finite-state characterization extends beyond two classes. This is not a polynomial-in-input-size complexity theorem.

progress.summary: Exact finite-state saturation criteria cover arbitrary finite class mixtures with Poisson arrivals and phase-type durations; compact/polynomial-complexity and broader-input targets remain distinct.

links.title: RESET and MARC (2023), model, saturation criterion, Theorem 4.2 and Appendix C

literature.synthesis: The missing distinction was between a compact formula and an exact characterization through a finite saturated CTMC. For phase-type durations and Poisson i.i.d.-marked arrivals, the latter is available, including correlated server need and duration. The finite state space can grow rapidly with server count; solving balance equations is not by itself a polynomial algorithm in the original input size. Renewal and general-duration extensions need their own argument.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Start from the existing saturated finite CTMC. Seek state-space compression, tractable subclasses, or complexity bounds rather than rederiving enumerability.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Distinguish polynomial complexity in the primitive input from polynomial complexity in an exponentially expanded CTMC. Do not transfer Poisson i.i.d.-mark results to superposed general renewal streams without checking the class-order process.

notes_for_maintainer: Audit 2026-11-09: full-text model, saturation discussion, Theorem 4.2 and Appendix C reviewed. Narrowed the outstanding target; no blanket resolved status for the general-input/polynomial-complexity question.
